title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 91–92
description: Contextual polysemy, lexical ambiguity and natural adjective–noun, verb–adverb, adverb–adjective and verb–object collocations at advanced level.
sourceNotice: Prepared for individual language study from the user-provided textbook. Vocabulary targets are grounded in the source teaching sections, exercises and answer key; all example sentences, translations and notes are independently composed and no textbook exercises or extended source passages are reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 91 teaching sections A–B, Language help and exercises 91.1–91.6; Unit 92 teaching sections A–D, Language help and exercises 92.1–92.5, plus relevant answer-key entries. Exercise-only target words are separately attributed.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is included only for individual short items where reasonably confident; longer phrases and uncertain IPA are left blank rather than guessed. No connected-speech transcription is implied.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing text, including titles, sections, notes and examples, is in English; Brazilian Portuguese is used only in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Read complete teaching and exercise pages and answer-key entries. Checked multi-sense distinctions, source-versus-exercise provenance, UK usage, collocations and original sample sentences. Reopened the output and validated canonical JSON structure, types, unique IDs and static word/sentence audio compatibility.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 files. VocabLab import, actual browser speech synthesis and speech recognition have not been tested. Polysemous terms and preferred collocations can vary by context, speaker and region.

units.title: Unit 91 — One word, many meanings
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 188–189 (PDF pages 190–191).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Meaning and usage · polysemy and wordplay
learningObjectives: Disambiguate the meanings and word classes of fair, flat, capital and mean in context.
Distinguish multiple senses of match, bill, set, post, mark and run, including common collocations.
Interpret drill and other context-dependent nouns accurately across professional and everyday settings.
Recognise how English polysemy creates ambiguity and humour.

sectionsChecked: A · Polysemy examples and grammatical senses
B · Benefits of recognising polysemy and Language help on drill

items.pt: polissemia; presença de vários sentidos em uma palavra
items.example: Recognising polysemy prevents misleading word-for-word translations.
items.note: A linguistic term for one word having more than one sense.

items.pt: homógrafo; palavra com mesma grafia e significado diferente
items.example: A homograph may have a completely unrelated meaning in another context.
items.note: The unit uses the term for words with identical spelling but different meanings; some homographs also differ in pronunciation.

items.example: The committee proposed a fair procedure for selecting candidates.
items.note: As an adjective, fair here means reasonable and equitable; not a public event.

items.example: Several independent publishers presented their titles at the book fair.
items.note: Fair as a noun names a public exhibition or market; unrelated in meaning to fair meaning just.

items.pt: tempo bom; tempo estável e agradável
items.example: The forecast predicts fair weather for the whole weekend.
items.note: Fair describes pleasant weather, usually without heavy rain.

items.example: People with very fair skin may need additional sun protection.
items.note: Fair means light-coloured, as with skin or hair.

items.example: Her exam results were fair rather than outstanding.
items.note: Fair here means adequate or satisfactory, not excellent or necessarily equitable.

items.example: The researcher rented a small flat near the university.
items.note: British English noun meaning an apartment; American English normally uses apartment.

items.example: A flat surface is essential when installing the precision instrument.
items.note: Adjective describing an even, level surface.

items.example: The agency charges a flat fee regardless of the number of pages.
items.note: Flat describes a fixed amount that does not vary with the quantity involved.

items.example: The melody begins on B flat in the second bar.
items.note: In music, flat lowers a note by a semitone; different from level or apartment.

items.pt: cinco minutos cravados; exatamente cinco minutos
items.example: She assembled the demonstration in five minutes flat.
items.note: Informal adverbial flat emphasises an exact or impressively short duration.

items.example: Complete the registration form in capital letters.
items.note: Capital as an adjective means uppercase in typography.

items.pt: capital de um país ou região
items.example: The conference took place in the country's capital city.
items.note: Capital is the city where a government is based.

items.example: The start-up needs additional capital before entering a new market.
items.note: Uncountable noun referring to money or assets available for investment.

items.example: The article discusses countries that have abolished capital punishment.
items.note: A legal term for the death penalty; capital does not mean financial here.

items.example: What does the abbreviation stand for, and what does it mean?
items.note: Verb expressing the meaning conveyed by a word, sign or action.

items.example: I didn't mean to interrupt your presentation.
items.note: Mean to + infinitive expresses intention rather than word meaning.

items.example: He is so mean with money that he refuses to contribute to shared costs.
items.note: In British English, mean can describe someone unwilling to spend money.

items.example: The mean temperature was calculated from hourly measurements.
items.note: Mean is the arithmetic average in a statistical context.

items.example: It was mean of him to mock her accent in public.
items.note: Mean can describe unkind behaviour; context distinguishes this from stinginess.

items.example: Please return the flat keys to reception before leaving.
items.note: Here flat is a noun modifier meaning apartment, showing how word class and context affect interpretation.

items.example: He struck a match to light the candle during the power cut.
items.note: Match is a small stick that produces a flame when struck.

items.pt: um adversário à altura de; alguém equivalente a
items.example: The young chess player was a match for the tournament champion.
items.note: A match for someone means an equal competitor, not a fire-lighting object.

items.example: Their skills complement each other so well that they're a match made in heaven.
items.note: An idiom for a particularly suitable pair or partnership.

items.example: The seabird used its long bill to collect food from the sand.
items.note: Bill can mean a bird's beak.

items.example: The hotel sent us a detailed bill after our stay.
items.note: A document stating how much money must be paid.

items.example: The proposed bill will be debated in parliament next month.
items.note: In politics, a bill is proposed legislation not yet enacted as law.

items.example: The department purchased a set of reference books for the laboratory.
items.note: Set as a noun is a collection of related items.

items.pt: marcar uma data; definir uma data
items.example: We should set a date for the project review before Friday.
items.note: Set as a verb means establish or decide on something.

items.example: He has very set opinions about how the organisation should operate.
items.note: Set as an adjective means firmly fixed and difficult to change.

items.example: She applied for a senior research post at the institute.
items.note: In recruitment, a post is a position or job.

items.example: A red post marks the entrance to the cycle route.
items.note: Post can mean an upright pole or marker.

items.example: You can post a question in the forum if the instructions are unclear.
items.note: Post is a verb meaning publish a message online.

items.pt: corrigir e dar nota a uma prova
items.example: The lecturer will mark the papers by the end of the week.
items.note: Mark as a verb means assess work and assign a grade.

items.pt: marca de um milhão; patamar de um milhão
items.example: Online registrations passed the million mark in September.
items.note: Mark as a noun can denote a numerical level or threshold.

items.example: There was a small ink mark on the document.
items.note: A mark is a visible spot, trace or stain.

items.example: She has successfully run a small design business for ten years.
items.note: Run can mean manage or operate an organisation.

items.pt: sair para correr; fazer uma corrida
items.example: I usually go for a run after finishing work.
items.note: Run as a countable noun can mean one session of running.

items.example: The heatwave caused a run on electric fans across the city.
items.note: A run on a product means unusually high demand over a short period.

items.pt: broca odontológica; instrumento de perfuração dentária
items.example: The dentist checked the drill before starting the procedure.
items.note: Drill here means a tool used to make holes in teeth.

items.pt: treinamento de marcha e movimentos militares
items.example: The recruits practised military drill every morning.
items.note: Drill means formal repetitive training in a military context.

items.example: A worker used a road drill to break up the old pavement.
items.note: Here drill is a powerful tool for breaking or boring into road surfaces.

items.pt: exercício mecânico e repetitivo de gramática
items.example: A short grammar drill helped students practise the new structure.
items.note: Drill means repetitive practice designed to develop automatic responses.

items.pt: lista de chamada; registro de frequência escolar
items.example: The teacher checked the school register at the beginning of class.
items.note: Here register is an attendance list, not a postal service.

items.pt: registrar uma encomenda no correio; enviar como correspondência registrada
items.example: We chose to register the parcel because it contained important documents.
items.note: Here register is a verb meaning to send using a recorded postal service with delivery safeguards.

items.example: The local exhibition attracted interest from several community groups.
items.note: Interest can mean attention, concern or enthusiasm.

items.example: The account pays interest on savings every quarter.
items.note: In banking, interest is money earned or charged on a principal sum.

items.example: Dice the carrots finely before adding them to the stew.
items.note: Dice is a verb meaning cut food into small cubes.

items.example: Roll the dice to determine which player starts.
items.note: Dice is the traditional plural of die; in informal modern English dice may also be singular.

items.example: Her powerful service won her several points in the match.
items.note: In tennis, service means the action of starting a point by serving the ball.

items.example: The restaurant received praise for its attentive customer service.
items.note: Service here means help or attention provided to customers.

items.example: The solicitor prepared evidence for the legal case.
items.note: A case is a matter being considered by lawyers or a court.

items.example: She placed the delicate instrument inside a protective case.
items.note: Case can mean a container, including a suitcase or equipment case.

items.example: The player carefully positioned the cue before taking the shot.
items.note: A cue is the long stick used to strike balls in snooker or billiards.

items.pt: deixa; sinal para entrar em cena ou falar
items.example: The actor waited for her cue before speaking.
items.note: A cue is a signal telling a performer when to act or speak.

items.pt: caiu a ficha; percebi de repente
items.example: It suddenly hit me that the calculations were based on the wrong units.
items.note: Figurative hit means suddenly come to understand something.

items.example: The ball hit the fence and bounced back onto the court.
items.note: Literal hit refers to physical contact or impact.

items.pt: grou; ave de pernas e pescoço longos
items.example: A crane was standing in the wetland near the river.
items.note: Crane can name a large bird, as in the unit's joke.

items.example: The building crew used a crane to lift the steel beams.
items.note: Crane can also name a machine for raising heavy objects.

items.example: Time flies when everyone is enjoying the conversation.
items.note: Flies is a verb meaning passes quickly in this idiom.

items.example: Fruit flies appeared when the bananas became overripe.
items.note: Flies is a plural noun naming insects; different grammatical function from time flies.

items.example: The winter jacket is filled with warm goose down.
items.note: Down as a noun means the soft feathers used in insulation.

items.pt: os preços subiram; preços em alta
items.example: Prices are up again after the supply shortage.
items.note: Up indicates a rise in amount or value, not physical location.

items.pt: os preços caíram; preços em baixa
items.example: Energy prices are down compared with last winter.
items.note: Down here means lower in price; contrasted with down meaning feathers.

units.title: Unit 92 — Collocation: which words go together
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 190–191 (PDF pages 192–193).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose conventional adjective–noun collocations instead of plausible but unnatural alternatives.
Use typical verb–adverb and adverb–adjective pairings, including emphatic intensifiers.
Apply verb–object collocations accurately in everyday and academic contexts.
Use restricted collocations from practice exercises such as personal effects, death toll and strong tea.

sectionsChecked: D · Verb–object collocations and Language help

items.pt: colocação lexical; combinação habitual de palavras
items.example: Studying collocation helps advanced learners write more naturally.
items.note: Words that characteristically occur together; the choice of partner is not always predictable.

items.example: A simulator is useful, but using the real thing requires different skills.
items.note: The conventional expression is the real thing rather than the genuine thing.

items.example: The specialist confirmed that the watch was the genuine article.
items.note: Use the genuine article for an authentic object, not the real article.

items.example: The chair began with a broad summary of the research findings.
items.note: Broad collocates with summary; wide summary is not normal.

items.example: The final report describes the experimental procedure in great detail.
items.note: Use great detail, not big detail, for a thorough description.

items.pt: adversário formidável; oponente difícil de vencer
items.example: The newcomer defeated a formidable opponent in the final round.
items.note: Formidable suggests someone difficult to overcome, often with respect rather than dislike.

items.example: The laboratory has built a formidable reputation for precision measurement.
items.note: Formidable with reputation suggests powerful recognition, sometimes intimidating.

items.example: Reconstructing the corrupted archive became a formidable task.
items.note: Formidable emphasises scale and difficulty, not necessarily impossibility.

items.example: Meeting the deadline with limited resources posed a formidable challenge.
items.note: A common adjective–noun combination for substantial difficulty.

items.example: We had to walk fast to reach the station before departure.
items.note: Fast can function as an adverb after walk; fastly is not a word.

items.example: She walked quickly through the corridor to answer the call.
items.note: Quickly naturally modifies walk; compare move swiftly.

items.example: The discussion moved swiftly from the initial proposal to the budget.
items.note: Swiftly is a natural adverb with move, in literal or figurative contexts.

items.pt: ter uma opinião forte sobre; importar-se muito com
items.example: The team feels strongly about protecting the participants' privacy.
items.note: Use feel strongly about something rather than feel powerfully about.

items.pt: lembrar-se corretamente; se não me falha a memória
items.example: If I remember rightly, the trial ended in early June.
items.note: A common hedging phrase; remember perfectly is not a natural substitute here.

items.example: The conditions in the temporary shelter were utterly appalling.
items.note: Utterly commonly intensifies extreme adjectives, often negative ones.

items.example: The initial sales figures were utterly dismal.
items.note: Dismal indicates something depressing or very disappointing.

items.example: The suggestion that we should skip all safety checks was utterly ridiculous.
items.note: Natural strong negative evaluation; very formal contexts may favour more neutral wording.

items.example: Completing the migration in one hour is utterly impossible.
items.note: Utterly strengthens an already extreme adjective.

items.example: By the end of the three-day conference, the organisers were utterly exhausted.
items.note: An idiomatic intensifier with a state of complete tiredness.

items.example: Repeating the test without changing the setup would be utterly pointless.
items.note: A natural negative collocation conveying no useful purpose.

items.example: Our original assumptions turned out to be utterly wrong.
items.note: Stronger than simply wrong; suitable for emphatic correction.

items.example: Tampering with the results would be utterly unacceptable.
items.note: Frequent in formal criticism and statements of standards.

items.example: Please raise your hand if you would like to ask a question.
items.note: Raise your hand is the conventional verb–object collocation in this context.

items.pt: criar filhos; constituir e sustentar uma família
items.example: They raised a family while working in different cities.
items.note: Raise here means bring up children; lift a family is wrong for this meaning.

items.pt: acessar um site; visitar uma página da internet
items.example: Visit the official website for the latest application instructions.
items.note: Natural verb–object pairing; visit does not imply physical travel.

items.pt: clicar em um site; abrir um site por clique
items.example: Click on the website shown in the search results to check the details.
items.note: Website can follow click on; more precisely, one normally clicks a link to open a site.

items.pt: dar uma olhada em um site; explorar um site
items.example: You should check out the website before choosing a course.
items.note: Informal phrase meaning look at or examine a website.

items.example: The company states that its bags are made from genuine leather.
items.note: Both real leather and genuine leather are normal; the latter is commonly used as a product label.

items.example: The simulator cannot reproduce every hazard drivers face in the real world.
items.note: The conventional phrase is the real world, not the genuine world.

items.example: She is a genuine person who keeps her promises and listens carefully.
items.note: Genuine describes sincerity and authenticity of character.

items.example: Passengers must collect their personal effects before leaving the cabin.
items.note: Effects in this phrase means belongings, not results or consequences.

items.example: He made a feeble attempt to explain the missing figures.
items.note: Feeble collocates with attempt and suggests little effort or effectiveness.

items.example: I was pretty anxious about the outcome of the interview.
items.note: Pretty is a common, informal degree adverb meaning fairly or quite.

items.example: The contradictory instructions left the students utterly bewildered.
items.note: An idiomatic adverb–adjective pairing describing complete confusion.

items.example: A brisk walk before work helps me wake up.
items.note: Brisk describes energetic movement; not the abrupt manner suggested by brusque.

items.pt: abrir o apetite; aumentar a fome
items.example: A short swim can sharpen your appetite before lunch.
items.note: A traditional collocation meaning make you feel hungrier.

items.pt: número de mortos; total de vítimas fatais
items.example: Officials revised the death toll after completing the search.
items.note: Toll here means number of deaths caused by an event.

items.example: We took a leisurely stroll through the botanical gardens.
items.note: Leisurely means relaxed and unhurried, not necessarily difficult or sluggish.

items.example: It's perfectly OK to request more time for the assignment.
items.note: Perfectly commonly means completely in this reassurance phrase.

items.pt: deixar dinheiro em testamento; legar recursos
items.example: She decided to bequeath money to a medical charity.
items.note: Formal verb for leaving something to someone or an organisation in a will.

items.pt: tirar o apetite; estragar a fome
items.example: Eating too many biscuits before dinner can spoil your appetite.
items.note: The usual verb is spoil, not attack or lower, in this expression.

items.example: The company designed a powerful car for long-distance travel.
items.note: Powerful is the standard adjective for a vehicle with strong engine performance.

items.example: She prefers strong tea with a little milk.
items.note: Strong tea refers to flavour or concentration; powerful tea is not usual.

items.example: The portrait depicts a woman with auburn hair.
items.note: Auburn typically describes reddish-brown hair, not carpets.

items.example: He gave me a doleful expression when he heard the disappointing news.
items.note: Doleful means mournful or sorrowful; commonly used with expression or look.

items.example: The lengthy meeting ended without a final decision.
items.note: Lengthy naturally describes extended duration, not the physical size of a room.
